result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.modular_product()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the modular product of this graph with another. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L34001-L34056){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.modular_product(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Modular product](/assets/graphs/modular-product.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G is a paw: a triangle A, B, C with a tail C–D. H is a 4-cycle 1, 2, 3, 4. The path D–C–B in G and the path 1–2–3 in H (accent; the rest muted) are the same induced subgraph. Their modular product has 16 nodes and 40 edges, and its largest clique, drawn on the right as D1, C2, B3 for the pairs (D, 1), (C, 2), (B, 3), has 3 nodes: the largest induced subgraph common to both graphs." width="100%"} The modular product has a node for every pair `(g, h)` and joins `(g, h)` to `(g', h')` (with `g != g'` and `h != h'`) when the two pairs "agree": `g`-`g'` and `h`-`h'` are both edges, or both non-edges. Its cliques correspond exactly to induced subgraphs common to both graphs, so finding a maximum clique in the modular product solves the maximum common induced subgraph problem, a staple of comparing molecules and other structures (see `max_clique()`). Both graphs must be undirected. The result is simple and unweighted (parallel edges in the factors are collapsed), with the same node numbering and labels as `cartesian_product()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second factor. Neither graph is modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new undirected graph with `n * m` nodes. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If either graph is directed. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Every pair of pairs is checked, $O(n^2 m^2)$ time, so the method suits small graphs, as the maximum common subgraph problem itself is NP-hard. A clique $\{(g_1, h_1), \ldots, (g_k, h_k)\}$ maps $g_i \mapsto h_i$ isomorphically between the induced subgraphs (Barrow and Burstall, 1976). Matches NetworkX's `modular_product`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The largest common induced subgraph of a triangle-with-tail and a 4-cycle has 3 nodes (a path), the size of the modular product's largest clique: ::: {#cb0c7fc6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec paw = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) paw.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D")]) square = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(4) product = paw.modular_product(square) len(product.max_clique()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3 ``` ::: :::
